questions.question: The structures of temples located in India are classified as phamsana and latina on the basis of which of their parts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shikhara**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The classification of temple structures into phamsana and latina styles is based on the design of the **Shikhara**.
 
• **Phamsana** temples generally have a broader base and a gradual incline, resembling a pyramid-like structure.
 
• **Latina** temples have a more curvilinear and vertical rising Shikhara, often resembling a beehive shape.
 
• These classifications are primarily found in North Indian temple architecture, specifically in the Nagara style.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Garbagriha:**

 
 
• The Garbagriha, or sanctum sanctorum, is the innermost chamber of a temple where the main deity is enshrined.
 
• It is the most sacred part of the temple and is usually located directly under the Shikhara.
 
 
 
• **Amalaka:**
 
 
• An Amalaka is a stone disk, often ribbed, placed atop the Shikhara.
 
• It symbolizes the fruit of the amla tree and represents the sun.
 
 
 
• **Mandap:**
 
 
• The Mandap is a pavilion or hall, often used for public rituals and ceremonies.
 
• It is typically located in front of the Garbagriha and may be open or enclosed.
 
 
 
• **Nagara Style:**
 
 
• The Nagara style is a distinct form of North Indian temple architecture characterized by its towering Shikharas.
 
• It contrasts with the Dravidian style found in South India, which features pyramidal towers and intricate sculptures.

questions.question: Which of the following is the major reservoir of carbon on earth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ocean**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The ocean is the largest reservoir of carbon on Earth, containing about 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere.
 
• Oceans absorb roughly one-quarter of the carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted by human activities each year.
 
• Marine organisms, such as phytoplankton, play a significant role in the oceanic carbon cycle by absorbing CO2 during photosynthesis.
 
• The deep ocean stores carbon for long periods, often over centuries, making it a crucial component of the global carbon cycle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carbon Cycle:**

 
 
• The carbon cycle is the process by which carbon is exchanged between the Earth's oceans, soil, rocks, and atmosphere.
 
• It includes processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and sedimentation.
 
• Understanding the carbon cycle is essential for predicting climate change and managing carbon emissions.
 
 
 
• **Phytoplankton:**
 
 
• Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae that form the base of the ocean food web.
 
• They absorb CO2 during photosynthesis and produce oxygen, contributing significantly to the oceanic carbon cycle.
 
 
 
• **Carbon Sequestration:**
 
 
• Carbon sequestration refers to the process of capturing and storing atmospheric CO2.
 
• Oceans, forests, and soil are natural carbon sinks that sequester carbon, helping to mitigate climate change.
 
 
 
• **Ocean Acidification:**
 
 
• Ocean acidification occurs when CO2 is absorbed by seawater, leading to chemical reactions that reduce pH levels.
 
• This process can harm marine life, particularly organisms with calcium carbonate shells or skeletons.

questions.question: If nominal GDP is ₹1,800 and real GDP is ₹1,000. What will be the value of GDP deflator?

GDP Deflator=(Nominal GDPReal GDP)×100\text{GDP Deflator} = \left(\frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}}\right) \times 100

Therefore,

GDP Deflator=(18001000)×100=180%

questions.question: At what degree from the epicentre does the seismograph record the arrival of P-waves but NOT S-waves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Beyond 145º**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Seismographs record the arrival of P-waves but not S-waves at angles beyond 145º from the earthquake's epicenter.
 
• This is due to the presence of the Earth's liquid outer core, which S-waves cannot travel through.
 
• P-waves, or primary waves, are compressional waves that can travel through both solid and liquid layers of the Earth.
 
• S-waves, or secondary waves, are shear waves and can only travel through solid materials.
 
• The shadow zone for S-waves is created because they are blocked by the liquid outer core.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seismology:**

 
 
• Seismology is the scientific study of earthquakes and the propagation of elastic waves through the Earth.
 
• It plays a crucial role in understanding the Earth's internal structure and dynamics.
 
 
 
• **Epicenter and Focus:**
 
 
• The epicenter is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus, where an earthquake originates.
 
• The focus is the location within the Earth where the earthquake rupture starts.
 
 
 
• **Types of Seismic Waves:**
 
 
• P-waves (Primary waves): Compressional waves that travel fastest through the Earth.
 
• S-waves (Secondary waves): Shear waves that travel slower than P-waves and cannot pass through liquids.
 
• Surface waves: Travel along the Earth's surface and generally cause the most damage during an earthquake.
 
 
 
• **Seismic Shadow Zones:**
 
 
• The area of the Earth that does not receive any direct P-waves is called the P-wave shadow zone, typically found between 104º and 140º from the earthquake's epicenter.
 
• The S-wave shadow zone extends from 104º to 180º, as S-waves are completely blocked by the liquid outer core.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are true about globalisation?

I. It is about integration with world economies

II. It promotes competition among producers

III. Appreciation of domestic currency improves exports
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1) Only I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Globalisation involves integration with world economies:** It includes the process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments worldwide. (Source: World Bank)
 
• **Promotes competition among producers:** Globalisation leads to increased competition as companies from different countries compete in the global market. (Source: OECD)
 
• **Appreciation of domestic currency:** Generally makes exports more expensive and less competitive, reducing export levels. (Source: International Monetary Fund)

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trade Liberalisation:** The removal or reduction of trade barriers or restrictions on the free exchange of goods between nations. (Source: World Trade Organization)
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI):** An investment made by a firm or individual in one country into business interests located in another country. (Source: UNCTAD)
 
• **Exchange Rates:** The value of one currency for the purpose of conversion to another. Affects international trade and investments. (Source: Federal Reserve)
 
• **Multinational Corporations (MNCs):** Companies that operate in multiple countries. They play a significant role in globalisation. (Source: Harvard Business Review)

questions.question: What was the fraction of sales price collected as tax under the Mauryans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**(1)/(10)**__.

__
 
• Under the Mauryan Empire, a fraction of the sales price collected as tax was **(1)/(10)**.
 
• This tax was known as **"Bhaga,"** which means a share or portion.
 
• The Mauryan administration was known for its **efficient revenue collection system**.
 
• Taxation was a primary source of revenue for the Mauryan state to maintain its large army and administrative machinery.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Arthashastra:**

 
 
• The Arthashastra, written by Kautilya (Chanakya), was a treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy during the Mauryan period.
 
• It provides detailed insights into the Mauryan taxation system, including the collection of taxes and duties.
 
 
 
• **Revenue Sources:**
 
 
• Other significant sources of revenue included taxes on land (Bhaga), tolls, customs duties, and fines.
 
• Land tax, which was usually one-sixth of the produce, was a major contributor to the state’s revenue.
 
 
 
• **Administration:**
 
 
• The Mauryan administration was highly centralized, with the king at the top, followed by ministers and other officials.
 
• Revenue officers, known as Samaharta, were responsible for the collection of taxes.
 
 
 
• **Infrastructure Development:**
 
 
• The revenue collected was used for infrastructure development, including the construction of roads, irrigation systems, and public buildings.
 
• The state also maintained granaries and warehouses to ensure food security.

questions.question: Hydrogenation of vegetable oils is catalysed by ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ni**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Nickel (Ni) is widely used as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
 
• The hydrogenation process helps to convert liquid oils into semi-solid forms, such as margarine and shortening.
 
• Nickel catalysts facilitate the addition of hydrogen atoms to the unsaturated carbon bonds in vegetable oils.
 
• This process increases the melting point of the oils, making them more stable and suitable for use in various food products.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrogenation Process**

 
 
• Hydrogenation is a chemical reaction that involves the addition of hydrogen (H₂) to another compound.
 
• It is commonly used in the food industry to convert unsaturated fats to saturated fats.
 
• This process helps to increase the shelf life and stability of food products.
 
 
 
• **Trans Fats**
 
 
• Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils can lead to the formation of trans fats.
 
• Trans fats are associated with an increased risk of heart disease and other health issues.
 
• Regulations in many countries now limit the use of trans fats in food products.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Catalysts**
 
 
• Other metals like platinum (Pt) and palladium (Pd) can also be used as catalysts in hydrogenation, but they are more expensive than nickel.
 
• Research is ongoing to develop more efficient and sustainable catalysts for industrial applications.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states that ‘The Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply the Principles in making laws’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 37**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 37** of the Indian Constitution specifies that the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
• It mandates that it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• Although the DPSPs are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, they are crucial for governance.
 
• These principles aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
 
• The Directive Principles act as guidelines to the central and state governments of India to frame laws and policies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**:

 
 
• DPSPs are enumerated in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, from Article 36 to Article 51.
 
• These principles have been inspired by the Directive Principles given in the Constitution of Ireland.
 
• The aim is to establish a just society in India, and they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
 
 
• **Non-Justiciable Nature**:
 
 
• Unlike Fundamental Rights, DPSPs are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.
 
• However, they are considered essential for the understanding and governance of the country.
 
 
 
• **Categories of DPSPs**:
 
 
• DPSPs are classified into three categories: Socialistic, Gandhian, and Liberal-Intellectual.
 
• Socialistic principles aim at providing social and economic justice.
 
• Gandhian principles reflect the vision of Mahatma Gandhi for a self-sufficient village economy.
 
• Liberal-Intellectual principles are based on liberal ideals of justice, liberty, and equality.
 
 
 
• **Relation with Fundamental Rights**:
 
 
• There has been a debate on the relationship between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs.
 
• Fundamental Rights are justiciable and legally enforceable, while DPSPs are not.
 
• However, the Supreme Court of India has often interpreted Fundamental Rights and DPSPs harmoniously.

questions.question: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is a flagship programme of the government of India, that was started in 2001 to achieve ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is the Government of India's flagship program for achieving Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE).
 
• Launched in 2001, SSA aims to provide free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14 years.
 
• The program focuses on bridging gender and social gaps in education.
 
• SSA is aligned with the mandate of the Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009, which makes education a fundamental right.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009:**

 
 
• Ensures free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years in India.
 
• Mandates 25% reservation for disadvantaged sections in private schools.
 
• Sets norms and standards for pupil-teacher ratios, infrastructure, and teacher qualifications.
 
 
 
• **Mid-Day Meal Scheme:**
 
 
• Provides free lunches on working days for children in primary and upper primary classes.
 
• Aims to improve nutritional status of children and encourage school attendance.
 
 
 
• **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020:**
 
 
• Aims to overhaul the Indian education system and improve the quality of education.
 
• Focuses on early childhood care and education, foundational literacy, and numeracy.
 
 
 
• **Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA):**
 
 
• Launched in 2009 to enhance access to secondary education and improve its quality.
 
• Aims to achieve a gross enrollment ratio of 100% in secondary education by 2030.

questions.question: The Finance Commission submits its report to the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Finance Commission of India is constituted by the President under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The primary function of the Finance Commission is to define the financial relations between the central government and the individual state governments.
 
• The Finance Commission submits its report to the President of India, who then presents it to the Parliament.
 
• The report contains recommendations on the distribution of tax revenues between the Union and the States and among the States themselves.
 
• The President lays the report of the Finance Commission along with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken upon the recommendations before each House of Parliament.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**

 
 
• The Finance Commission is a constitutional body, as per Article 280 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It is appointed every five years to recommend measures and methods on how revenues need to be distributed between the Centre and states.
 
 
 
• **Composition:**
 
 
• The Finance Commission consists of a Chairman and four other members appointed by the President of India.
 
• The members should have expertise in public affairs, finance, and administration.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The first Finance Commission was established in 1951, and till now, several commissions have been constituted to address fiscal federalism in India.
 
 
 
• **Recent Developments:**
 
 
• The 15th Finance Commission, chaired by N.K. Singh, was constituted in 2017 and submitted its report for 2021-2026.
 
• Recent recommendations include the allocation of funds for disaster management and health sector improvement.

questions.question: Which among the following states has the lowest poverty ratio as per the Multidimensional Poverty Index (2021) of the NITI Aayog?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Kerala has the lowest poverty ratio in India as per the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) report by NITI Aayog in 2021.
 
• The state recorded a poverty ratio of only 0.71%, the lowest among all Indian states.
 
• This low poverty ratio is attributed to Kerala's robust social welfare schemes and high human development indicators.
 
• Kerala has consistently performed well in areas such as health, education, and standard of living, contributing to its low poverty levels.
 
• The state's effective implementation of public policies and high literacy rates are key factors in reducing poverty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**

 
 
• MPI is an international measure of acute multidimensional poverty covering over 100 developing countries.
 
• It identifies multiple deprivations at the household and individual level in health, education, and standard of living.
 
• Developed by the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
 
• NITI Aayog's MPI report is an important tool for formulating poverty alleviation policies in India.
 
 
 
• **Kerala's Social Welfare Programs**
 
 
• Kerala has numerous social security schemes like the Kudumbashree program aimed at women empowerment and poverty eradication.
 
• The state offers comprehensive healthcare services through its primary health centers and the Aardram Mission.
 
• High literacy rates are maintained through initiatives such as the Akshara Keralam project focusing on adult education.
 
• The Public Distribution System (PDS) in Kerala ensures food security for its citizens.
 
 
 
• **Human Development Index (HDI)**
 
 
• HDI is a composite index measuring average achievement in three basic aspects of human development: health, education, and income.
 
• Kerala has consistently scored high on HDI due to its effective social policies.
 
• It provides insights into long-term progress in various dimensions of human development.
 
 
 
• **Economic Indicators in Kerala**
 
 
• Kerala's economy is driven by sectors such as tourism, remittances from the diaspora, and agriculture.
 
• The state has a relatively high per capita income compared to other Indian states.
 
• Investments in education and health have resulted in a skilled and healthy workforce.

questions.question: The ‘Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana’ (VAMBAY) was launched in which year by the Government of India?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The 'Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana' (VAMBAY) was launched in the year **2001** by the Government of India.
 
• It was initiated under the Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation.
 
• The scheme aims to provide shelter or upgrade the existing shelter for people living below the poverty line in urban slums.
 
• VAMBAY also focuses on improving the living conditions of slum dwellers by providing better sanitation facilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY)**

• The scheme provides interest subsidies on home loans under the Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS).

• Renamed as Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G) in 2016.
 
• It aims to provide a pucca house with basic amenities to all houseless households and those living in kutcha and dilapidated houses.

questions.question: The Teesta low dam is located in which of the following states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sikkim**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Teesta Low Dam is situated in the state of **Sikkim**, India.
 
• It is located on the **Teesta River**, which is one of the major rivers in Sikkim.
 
• The dam is part of a hydroelectric project aimed at generating **hydropower** for the region.
 
• The project is crucial for meeting the energy needs of Sikkim and neighboring regions.
 
• The Teesta Low Dam Hydroelectric Project is managed by **NHPC Limited**, a Government of India enterprise.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Teesta River:**

 
 
• The Teesta River originates from the **Tso Lhamo Lake** in North Sikkim.
 
• It flows through Sikkim and West Bengal before merging with the Brahmaputra River in Bangladesh.
 
• The river is vital for irrigation, drinking water, and hydroelectric projects in the region.
 
 
 
• **Hydropower in Sikkim:**
 
 
• Sikkim has abundant water resources, making it an ideal location for hydroelectric projects.
 
• Hydropower is a major source of renewable energy in Sikkim, contributing significantly to the state's energy supply.
 
• Several hydropower projects, including the Teesta Low Dam, are operational in the state.
 
 
 
• **NHPC Limited:**
 
 
• NHPC Limited (National Hydroelectric Power Corporation) is a premier organization in India dedicated to the development of hydropower.
 
• It was incorporated in 1975 and has since been a key player in the hydroelectric sector.
 
• NHPC manages multiple hydroelectric projects across India, including the Teesta Low Dam.
 
 
 
• **Sikkim's Geography:**
 
 
• Sikkim is a mountainous state in northeastern India, known for its diverse terrain and scenic landscapes.
 
• It shares borders with Nepal to the west, Tibet to the north and northeast, Bhutan to the east, and West Bengal to the south.
 
• The state's topography makes it suitable for hydropower projects, which harness the energy of its fast-flowing rivers.

questions.question: The main source of ocean heat is __________.

__
 
• Sunlight is the primary source of heat for the Earth's oceans.
 
• Solar radiation penetrates the ocean surface, warming the water and contributing to temperature variations.
 
• The energy from sunlight drives oceanic currents and influences global climate patterns.
 
• Approximately 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by oceans, and sunlight is crucial for maintaining their thermal balance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Greenhouse Effect**

 
 
• The greenhouse effect is a process where certain gases in the Earth's atmosphere trap heat, leading to a warming effect.
 
• It helps maintain the Earth's temperature but excessive greenhouse gases can lead to global warming.
 
 
 
• **Ocean Currents**
 
 
• Ocean currents are large-scale movements of water within the world's oceans, driven by wind, water density differences, and the Coriolis effect.
 
• They play a key role in regulating the Earth's climate by redistributing heat around the planet.
 
 
 
• **Thermocline**
 
 
• The thermocline is a distinct layer in the ocean where the temperature gradient is steeper than the layers above and below it.
 
• It acts as a barrier to the mixing of surface and deep water layers, affecting marine life and nutrient distribution.
 
 
 
• **Albedo Effect**
 
 
• The albedo effect refers to the reflectivity of the Earth's surface; higher albedo surfaces reflect more sunlight, reducing heat absorption.
 
• Oceans have a low albedo, meaning they absorb more heat compared to land or ice-covered surfaces.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty?

options.text: To pay income tax in time

__
 
• **Fundamental Duties** are enshrined in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution under Article 51A.
 
• The Fundamental Duties were added by the **42nd Amendment Act in 1976** on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• There are **eleven Fundamental Duties** listed in the Indian Constitution.
 
• Paying income tax in time is **not listed** as one of the Fundamental Duties.
 
• Fundamental Duties include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, and safeguarding public property among others.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 51A** of the Indian Constitution outlines the Fundamental Duties of every citizen of India.
 
• The Fundamental Duties emphasize the importance of a citizen's responsibility towards the nation.
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act**, which introduced the Fundamental Duties, is often referred to as the "mini-Constitution" due to the extensive changes it brought.
 
• The concept of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution was inspired by the Constitution of the former Soviet Union.
 
• Unlike Fundamental Rights, the Fundamental Duties are **non-justiciable**, meaning they are not enforceable by the courts.

questions.question: Name the employee of the East India Company who deciphered Asokan Brahmi in 1830s.

questions.question: Which of the following Statutory Commissions was set up to study the working of the government after the Government of India Act 1919 was passed?

__
 
• The Simon Commission was constituted in **1927** to review the working of the constitutional system in India as per the Government of India Act 1919.
 
• It was a seven-member commission chaired by **Sir John Simon**.
 
• The commission was boycotted by Indian political parties because it did not include any Indian members.
 
• The report of the Simon Commission led to the Government of India Act 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy and the establishment of federal courts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
 
• Introduced a dual system of governance (dyarchy) in the provinces.
 
• Separate electorates were expanded and more power was given to the provincial legislative councils.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act 1935**
 
 
• This act provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation.
 
• It introduced provincial autonomy, allowing elected Indian representatives to form governments.
 
• It also established a federal court and expanded the franchise.
 
 
 
• **Butler Commission**
 
 
• Set up in 1927 to examine the relationship between the princely states and the British Crown.
 
• Recommended that the relationship should be direct and not through the Government of India.
 
 
 
• **Hunter Commission**
 
 
• Formed in 1919 to investigate the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

questions.question: Which mountain range includes the Shiwalik range as a part?

• The elevation of the Shiwalik range varies from 600 meters to 1200 meters.

• The range is divided into three parallel ranges: the Greater Himalayas, the Lesser Himalayas, and the Shiwalik range.
 
 
 
• **Geological Formation:**
 
 
• The Himalayas were formed as a result of the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
 
• This process started approximately 50 million years ago and continues to this day, making the Himalayas a geologically active region.
 
 
 
• **Flora and Fauna:**

questions.question: Which state of the matter has LEAST force of attraction between its particles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gases have the least force of attraction between their particles compared to solids, liquids, and plasma.
 
• The particles in a gas are widely spaced and move freely and rapidly in all directions.
 
• This weak force of attraction allows gases to fill any container they are placed in, taking the shape and volume of the container.
 
• Due to minimal intermolecular forces, gases can be compressed easily and have low densities.
 
• The kinetic energy of gas particles is higher than that of solids and liquids, leading to greater movement and lower attraction between particles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Solid State**:

 
 
• In solids, particles are closely packed in a fixed, orderly arrangement, resulting in strong intermolecular forces of attraction.
 
• This strong attraction gives solids a definite shape and volume.
 
 
 
• **Liquid State**:
 
 
• Liquids have a moderate level of attraction between particles, allowing them to flow and take the shape of their container while retaining a fixed volume.
 
• The particles in a liquid are less tightly packed than in a solid but are closer together than in a gas.
 
 
 
• **Plasma State**:
 
 
• Plasma consists of highly energized particles with sufficient energy to overcome the attraction between electrons and nuclei, resulting in a collection of free-moving ions and electrons.
 
• It is often referred to as the fourth state of matter and is found in stars, including the sun, and in man-made objects like neon signs and plasma TVs.
 
 
 
• **Kinetic Theory of Gases**:
 
 
• This theory explains the behavior of gases based on the idea that gas particles are in constant, random motion and that their collisions with the walls of a container cause pressure.
 
• It also states that the temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its particles.

questions.question: The Stupa sculptures found at Sanghol in Punjab belongs to which of the following schools?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mathura**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Stupa sculptures found at Sanghol in Punjab belong to the **Mathura school of art**.
 
• The Mathura school of art is known for its distinctive style characterized by the depiction of Buddha in human form and elaborate decorative elements.
 
• The sculptures from Mathura exhibit a strong sense of movement and vitality, often showcasing intricate carvings and detailed drapery.
 
• The Mathura school flourished during the Kushan period, particularly under the patronage of rulers like Kanishka.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gandhara School of Art**:

 
 
• The Gandhara school emerged in the region of modern-day Pakistan and Afghanistan during the Kushan period.
 
• It is renowned for its Greco-Roman influence, evident in the realistic representation of human figures and drapery.
 
• This school primarily used grey schist stone for its sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Sarnath School of Art**:
 
 
• Sarnath, near Varanasi, became an important center for Buddhist art during the Gupta period.
 
• The sculptures from Sarnath are noted for their serene and compassionate expressions, depicting Buddha in a more spiritual and ethereal manner.
 
• Polished sandstone was commonly used in the Sarnath school.
 
 
 
• **Amravati School of Art**:
 
 
• The Amravati school flourished in the Andhra region, particularly around the Krishna River, during the Satavahana period.
 
• It is known for its dynamic and detailed narrative panels depicting scenes from the life of Buddha.
 
• White marble was often used for the sculptures from this school.

questions.question:
Select the correct sequence of the following steps during the process of photosynthesis.

i. Chlorophyll helps in absorbing light energy.

ii. Light energy is converted into chemical energy and the water molecule is split into oxygen and hydrogen molecules.

iii. Carbon dioxide is converted into carbohydrates.

options.text: Step i and step ii always occur together and step iii can occur any other time
They always occur sequentially in the order i −> ii −> iii
Step i occurs first and steps ii and iii occur together next
These steps need not occur one after another immediately

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They always occur sequentially in the order i -> ii -> iii**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During photosynthesis, light energy is first absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts, initiating the process.
 
• The absorbed light energy is then converted into chemical energy, leading to the splitting of water molecules into oxygen and hydrogen.
 
• Oxygen is released as a by-product of the splitting of water molecules.
 
• The hydrogen molecules are used in the Calvin cycle to convert carbon dioxide into carbohydrates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chlorophyll:** A green pigment found in the chloroplasts of plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, responsible for the absorption of light energy during photosynthesis.
 
• **Calvin Cycle:** Also known as the light-independent reactions or dark reactions, this cycle uses ATP and NADPH produced in the light-dependent reactions to fix carbon dioxide into carbohydrates.
 
• **Photosystems:** Complexes of chlorophyll and proteins in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts that play a crucial role in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
 
• **ATP and NADPH:** These are energy carriers produced during the light-dependent reactions and are used in the Calvin cycle to synthesize carbohydrates.
 
• **Stomata:** Small openings on the surface of leaves that allow the exchange of gases (CO₂ and O₂) necessary for photosynthesis.
